title: Peddi Is Ram Charan's Biggest Solo Hit Ever. So Why Did the Makers Quietly Re-Cut It Mid-Run?
excerpt: The sports drama crossed ₹400 crore worldwide and gave the Mega Power Star his career-best solo number. Then a consent controversy over Janhvi Kapoor's character forced an apology, fresh scenes, and a re-release — a first for a film this size.
body:
The numbers tell one story. Ram Charan walks onto the screen in **Peddi** as an *aata coolie* — a player for hire from a village that doesn't even have a name on the map — and by the time the dust settles, he has wrestled, batted, and sprinted his way into the record books. By Day 14, the film had crossed ₹225 crore net in India and, by its makers' count, ₹400 crore worldwide. It is now the highest-grossing Telugu film of 2026, the highest-grossing South Indian film of the year, and — the line that matters most to the **Mega Power Star** himself — his biggest solo hit ever, eclipsing even the beloved *Rangasthalam*.


<youtube></youtube>

The other story is the one nobody at Vriddhi Cinemas wanted to tell.

Directed by **Buchi Babu Sana** — the man who gave Telugu cinema the gut-punch of *Uppena* — *Peddi* arrived on June 4 carrying the weight of a pan-India dream. Charan plays a cricketer-for-hire who fights for the dignity of a community without a name, moving from cricket to *kushti* to the sprint track in a search for recognition. The ambition is enormous; the canvas, rural Vizianagaram, is gorgeously shot. Early reviews praised the emotional sweep.

Then, within forty-eight hours, the conversation curdled.

> "It's high time they stop sexualising heroines in films. There's a scene where the hero describes her face but they show her waist and chest." — A viewer on X

The lightning rod was **Janhvi Kapoor**'s character, Achiyamma. A steamy power-cut kiss went viral first. But the anger quickly moved past one scene and onto the architecture of the role itself: critics argued Achiyamma was all style and no agency, introduced through lingering shots of her body rather than any sense of who she was. One sequence — in which a goon undresses her in public during an election campaign while the hero watches — drew particular fury. "Objectification" trended for two straight days. Academics weighed in. Reddit threads lit up. Janhvi's own make-up artist, **Savleen Kaur Manchanda**, took to Instagram to suggest the actress had objected to some shots during post-production.

What happened next is genuinely rare in an industry that usually lets a controversy burn itself out while the cash registers ring. Buchi Babu didn't go quiet. He went on X and apologised.

> "Cinema should entertain, inspire, and connect with audiences. It should never make anyone feel uncomfortable or disrespected. We have heard the feedback regarding certain scenes in Peddi and have taken it seriously." — Buchi Babu Sana

He admitted he hadn't anticipated the reaction. "The idea was to showcase a playful romance," he told *SCREEN*, "but we'll be more careful and make better representations." Then he did something almost unheard of for a film this size: he ordered the objectionable shots cut, had two-to-three alternative scenes reinstated to give Achiyamma actual narrative weight, and pushed a **re-edited version back into theatres from June 17** — while the film was still mid-run and still minting money.

Think about the economics of that. *Peddi* opened with over ₹100 crore on Day 1 — a first for Charan as a solo lead — and held strong through a second weekend, selling 92,000 tickets on its second Friday alone, the sixth-best second-Friday BookMyShow figure in Tollywood history. To re-cut a film clearing ₹9 crore a day is not a small gesture. It is a studio blinking.

For the diaspora, *Peddi* has been a familiar kind of event. Overseas premieres pulled in $1.57 million — Charan's second-best ever after *RRR* — and North American advance sales for opening weekend hit $1.37 million. The film is playing across the US, UK, Canada and Australia in **Telugu, Hindi, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam**, with the Telugu version carrying nearly 80% of the load. If you're in New Jersey or Toronto and catching a later show this week, you may well be watching the kinder, recut Achiyamma — the version that exists only because the internet refused to look away.

So here's the take. *Peddi* is a hit by every metric Charan has ever chased, and a long-overdue reckoning for how South cinema frames its heroines, all in the same breath. The milestone will go in the record books. But the more interesting legacy might be the apology — proof that even a Mega Power Star vehicle can be made to flinch when the audience decides a woman on screen deserves to be more than a camera angle.
